One-page synthesis

The article describes three children with optic nerve aplasia, a rare congenital absence of the optic nerve and retinal vasculature. The cases show substantial clinical variation. Case 1 had unilateral right disease with profound visual loss, exotropia, enophthalmos, and no detected brain anomaly. Case 2 had unilateral left disease with partial aniridia, chorioretinal atrophy, and markedly elevated left intraocular pressure. Case 3 had bilateral disease with microcornea, iris and lens coloboma, absent optic nerves and chiasm, but no brain abnormality on MRI.

The source is useful for phenotype recognition and for showing that bilateral optic nerve aplasia does not invariably coincide with a visible brain malformation in a single reported patient. It does not estimate prevalence, prognosis, diagnostic-test performance, or treatment effect. The authors recommend systemic evaluation and neuroimaging to look for associated central nervous system and endocrine abnormalities, but the three-case design cannot establish the benefit, yield, or current standard of that strategy.

Section-by-section review

Abstract and introduction

The authors define optic nerve aplasia by congenital absence of the optic nerve head, retinal vessels, retinal ganglion cells, and optic nerve fibers in a blind eye. They frame unilateral disease as more often occurring without major brain abnormalities and bilateral disease as more often associated with central nervous system abnormalities. The article's stated purpose is to report three cases with varied presentations.

The background discussion relies on cited literature rather than data generated by this series. Those claims should remain secondary context until the cited primary reports are read directly.

Case 1

A 6-year-old girl had no perception of light in the right eye, pseudoptosis, a total afferent pupillary defect, 50 prism diopters of exotropia, and relative enophthalmos. The right fundus lacked an optic nerve and retinal vessels and showed chorioretinal atrophy. The left eye had 20/20 vision and normal findings.

Ultrasound, CT, and MRI supported absence of the orbital portion of the right optic nerve. The authors did not identify a significant brain abnormality. The case documents unilateral disease without an associated brain anomaly in the imaging reported.

Case 2

A 5-year-old child had no perception of light in the left eye. The left eye had partial aniridia and complete absence of the optic nerve and retinal vessels with macular and mid-peripheral chorioretinal atrophy. Intraocular pressure was 50 mmHg in the left eye and 12 mmHg in the right eye by applanation tonometry.

The right eye had a prior trauma and surgical history, which complicates interpretation of contralateral ocular findings. The article treats the left-eye pressure finding as associated glaucoma, but the case cannot establish a causal relation between optic nerve aplasia and glaucoma.

Case 3

A 5-month-old girl who had not developed a social smile did not fix or follow light. She had bilateral microcornea, a persistent pupillary membrane in the right eye, and iris and lens coloboma in the left eye. Both fundi lacked optic nerve heads and retinal blood vessels.

MRI showed bilateral absence of the optic nerves and chiasm with no reported brain abnormality. The authors consider this presentation unusual because their background model links bilateral disease more often with central nervous system abnormalities.

Discussion and conclusion

The discussion reviews proposed embryologic mechanisms and associated ocular and systemic abnormalities. The authors state that 38 cases had been reported by that time, but they do not describe a systematic literature-search method. This number is best read as a historical author-reported count, not a reproducible prevalence estimate.

The authors recommend systemic evaluation and neuroimaging to assess for central nervous system malformations and endocrine abnormalities. They also mention ocular prosthesis, shatterproof glasses, mobility training, and vocational rehabilitation. These recommendations are clinically plausible management statements from the source, but this case series does not compare diagnostic or rehabilitation strategies.

Disclosures

The authors report appropriate patient consent, no financial support or sponsorship, and no conflicts of interest.

Figures

Figure 1, Case 1

Purpose: show the absent right optic nerve head and retinal vessels, the normal contralateral fundus, and the expected orbital location of the absent right optic nerve on coronal MRI. The image supports the anatomic case description but does not provide a quantitative diagnostic comparison.

Figure 2, Case 2

Purpose: contrast a normally appearing right fundus with the left fundus lacking a visible optic nerve and retinal vessels. The figure documents morphology in one patient.

Figure 3, Case 3

Purpose: show bilateral absence of the optic nerve heads and retinal vessels and the MRI appearance of bilateral optic nerve absence. The figure is central to the authors' description of bilateral disease without a reported brain abnormality.

Evaluation and appraisal

Verdict: Skim deeply. Read the cases and figures for phenotype recognition. Do not use this source alone to set current diagnostic, endocrine-screening, or rehabilitation practice.

Clinical question

What clinical, ocular, and neuroimaging patterns were observed in three children with optic nerve aplasia? There was no intervention or comparator. The outcomes were descriptive ophthalmic examination and imaging findings.

Bias and uncertainty

Selection bias is the main concern because the source does not explain how the cases were identified. Reporting bias is also possible because unusual phenotypes are more likely to be published. The article provides no longitudinal follow-up, no denominator of evaluated patients, and no systematic method for its historical literature count.

Do not interpret the association between unilateral or bilateral optic nerve aplasia and specific systemic abnormalities as a frequency estimate from this series. Those statements come from cited literature and were not tested in these three patients.

Implementation and practice takeaways

Use the source for
Case recognition, image-based morphology, and historical examples of unilateral and bilateral optic nerve aplasia.
Do not use the source for
Prevalence, causal claims, prognosis estimates, diagnostic-test yield, or treatment efficacy.
Current-practice boundary
The source is from 2018. Current clinical decisions should be checked against newer ophthalmology, neuroimaging, and endocrine guidance before use.
Read next
The 10 cited sources are preserved in the companion Markdown task queue. Primary articles should be read directly before their findings become primary LiteratureAtoms.
